podcast.title: Advertising Commercial for Old Home Bread (1973)
podcast.body: Bill Freese, using the persona C. W. McCall, created a TV commercial for Old Home Bread. It featured McCall as a truck driver and a waitress named Mavis at the Old Home and Fillarepp Cafe. The commercial won a Clio, the highest award for an advertisement, and was noted for Mavis's seductive portrayal, which would likely not be made today. "That commercial won a Clio, the highest possible award for an advertising commercial or advertisement, and would never be made today as Mavis pretty much seduces C. W and kept him, quote, warm as toast while the blizzard raged outside."

podcast.title: Fictional Artist Creation (1973)
podcast.body: C. W. McCall was not a real artist but a fictional recording persona invented by an ad campaign for Old Home Bread in 1973. Bill Freeze was the creative director who conceived and voiced the trucker character, with Chip Davis providing the music, making him a unique commercial-to-music success story. "an artist who wasn't even real. The number one hit that resulted from this artist wasn't an ad in itself, but without advertising, the whole thing never would have happened in the first place."

podcast.title: Film Adaptation (1978)
podcast.body: The immense popularity of the song "Convoy" led to a movie adaptation two years later, starring Chris Christofferson and Ali McGraw and directed by Sam Peckinpah. This film further solidified the song's cultural impact, grossing nearly $50 million at the box office. "It spawned a movie two years later starring Chris Christofferson and Ali McGraw and directed by Sam Peckinpaw."

podcast.title: Chip Davis's Dislike for Country Music
podcast.body: Despite "Convoy" becoming a six-week number one hit on Billboard's Hot Country Singles chart, its co-creator Chip Davis paradoxically declared that he didn't even like country music, adding an ironic twist to the song's massive success in the genre. "Which was kind of funny because Chip Davis declared that he didn't even like country music."

podcast.title: Country and Western Character
podcast.body: The "C. W." in C. W. McCall specifically stood for Country and Western, reflecting the character's persona as a trucker who loved bread, which was central to the Old Home Bread ad campaign. "The C. W. stood for Country and Western."

podcast.body: C.W. McCall died on April 1st at the age of 93 from cancer. "He died on April 1st at the age of 93. He had cancer."

podcast.title: MGM Records Distribution
podcast.body: Following the regional success of "Old Home Filler Up and Keep a Truck in the Cafe" on Chip Davis's independent American Gramophone label, the major label MGM Records took notice and signed C. W. McCall to provide national distribution, leading to the broader success of "Convoy." "The major label MGM records took notice and signed C. W. McCall to provide national distribution."

podcast.title: Novelty Song Hit
podcast.body: C.W. McCall, whose real name was Billy Dale Fries, had a weird hit in the 1970s with the novelty song "Convoy." "Remember the novelty song Convoy from the 1970s? That was a weird hit by an award-winning American ad executive named Billy Dale Freeze."
